input.question: How does an orphaned oil well become a public problem decades after the company that drilled it disappears?

research_context.universe_question: What happens after a mine, dam, cable, factory, or software system is no longer useful to its original owner but remains physically or institutionally present?
research_context.distinct_engine: The environmental and financial afterlife of extraction is more about legal disappearance than physical drilling; plugging costs land on the public.
research_context.evidence_needed: Well registries, corporate histories, state orphan well programs, inspection reports, financial assurance records.
research_context.second_act: The same legal-disappearance mechanism leaves the public holding reclamation costs at abandoned coal mines and orphaned Superfund sites, so the oil-well story opens into a broader afterlife-of-extraction pattern.

value.title: 42 U.S. Code § 15907 — Orphaned well site plugging, remediation, and restoration
value.publisher: Cornell Law School / Legal Information Institute (U.S. Code)
value.note: The federal statute creating the orphaned-well program. Defines 'orphaned well' as a well for which no operator can be located or whose operator is unable to plug and reclaim the site — the legal-disappearance definition at the heart of the mechanism. Sets initial/formula/performance grant amounts ($25M initial, $20M regulatory-improvement caps) and requires public cost accounting.

value.title: California Public Resources Code § 3206.3 — idle and orphan well reporting
value.note: State statute requiring an annual public report listing idle wells, orphan wells, estimated costs of abandoning orphan wells, and a plugging timeline. Defines an orphan well as one 'that has no party responsible for it, leaving the state to plug and abandon it' — a well registry/accountability record.

value.title: Oil and Gas Wells: Bureau of Land Management Needs to Improve Its Data and Oversight of Its Potential Liabilities (GAO-18-250)
value.note: GAO audit explaining why cleanup costs land on the public: BLM did not systematically track reclamation costs or orphan-well counts, so it could not assure bonds cover the liability. Figures: known orphaned wells rose from 144 (2010) to 219 (2017); average annual reclamation cost $267,600. An audit of the financial-assurance gap.

value.title: Oil and Gas Bonds: Bonding Requirements and BLM Expenditures to Reclaim Orphaned Wells (GAO-10-245)
value.note: GAO audit quantifying the number, value, and coverage of BLM bonds versus what BLM has paid to reclaim orphaned wells over 20 years and how many remain unreclaimed — direct evidence on the bond-vs-cost shortfall that shifts plugging costs to federal dollars.

value.title: Reclaiming Abandoned Mine Lands (Title IV of SMCRA)
value.publisher: Office of Surface Mining Reclamation and Enforcement (U.S. Dept. of the Interior)
value.note: Second-act parallel: coal operators disappeared before 1977 SMCRA, so reclamation is publicly funded via a per-ton fee. Figures: AML Fund has collected $14.233 billion, distributed $6.569 billion in grants — same legal-disappearance structure as orphaned wells.

value.title: Billion Dollar Orphans: Why millions of oil and gas wells could become wards of the state
value.note: Analysis explaining the causal mechanism: bonding amounts are set far below plugging cost, so when operators disappear the public inherits liability. Figures: 2.6M documented + ~1.2M undocumented unplugged onshore wells; ~$280B plugging cost; states hold surety bonds covering less than 1% of that.

value.title: Fiscal Responsibility — Orphan Well Association (Alberta)
value.note: A non-U.S. orphan-well authority's own statement of how it is funded after operators vanish: industry levy since 2002 ($1.14B collected; 2026/27 levy ~$155M) and average decommissioning cost $28,800 per well. Shows the public/industry-carried cost after legal disappearance of operators.

value.title: Superfund: Litigation Has Decreased and EPA Needs Better Information on Site Cleanup and Cost Issues (GAO-09-656)
value.publisher: U.S. Government Accountability Office (via UNT Digital Library)
value.note: Second-act evidence with figures: EPA lacks comprehensive data on orphan shares, and 13% (183 of 1,397) nonfederal NPL sites had no responsible parties identified as of FY2007 — i.e., the public is left holding cleanup where the responsible party has disappeared.
